label: HISTORY
title: Shackleton's Endurance: A Crushed Ship, an 800-Mile Lifeboat Voyage and No Lives Lost
description: In 1915 the ship Endurance was trapped and crushed by Antarctic sea ice, leaving 28 men on a drifting floe with no way to call for help. What followed was 18 months of survival, a 1,300-kilometre voyage in a lifeboat across the stormiest ocean on Earth, and a rescue in which every man of the crew came home.

chapters.heading: Introduction
image_queries: Endurance ship trapped in ice Hurley

lines.t: Jack, here is a plan. Sail to Antarctica, walk across the entire continent, about three thousand kilometres, and get picked up on the other side.
In 1914? With dogs and wooden sledges?
Exactly that. It was called the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, and its leader was Ernest Shackleton.
Did they make it across?
They never even set foot on the continent. The ship was caught by the ice before it could land.
So it was a failure.
As an expedition, completely. As a story of leadership, it may be the greatest of the polar age. Twenty-eight men went into the ice on that ship, and twenty-eight came out.
The ship was called Endurance. She left England in August 1914, in the very week the First World War began.
And nobody stopped them?
Shackleton offered the ship to the navy. He was told to proceed.
Their last port was a whaling station on South Georgia, a remote island in the South Atlantic. The whalers warned that the ice was unusually heavy that year.
He went anyway.
On the 5th of December 1914. For six weeks Endurance pushed through pack ice in the Weddell Sea. By mid-January they were within about a day's sail of their landing place.
And then?
The temperature dropped, the ice closed, and the ship was frozen solid. One crew member said she was stuck like an almond in a chocolate bar.
There was nothing to do but wait for spring. The ship drifted with the ice for nine months.
What did the men do all winter?
Shackleton understood that boredom and despair were as dangerous as cold. He kept strict routines. They trained the dogs, played football on the ice, held concerts.
The expedition photographer, Frank Hurley, took some of the most famous images in exploration. The ship lit by flares in the polar night.
But spring did not free them.
It did the opposite. As the ice began to move, it squeezed. Beams cracked. The deck buckled. On the 27th of October 1915, Shackleton gave the order to abandon ship.
They camped on the ice beside her. On the 21st of November they watched Endurance go under.
So now they are standing on frozen sea.
Hundreds of kilometres from land, with three lifeboats, and nobody in the world knowing where they are.
They tried marching, dragging the boats. It was hopeless. So they camped and let the ice carry them north.
For how long?
More than five months. They ate seals and penguins. When food ran short, the sled dogs had to be shot.
That must have hit morale.
Shackleton managed people carefully. He put the most difficult men in his own tent, so they could not spread discontent.
By April 1916 the floe was breaking apart beneath them. On the 9th of April they launched the three boats.
Toward where?
The nearest land they could reach. After about a week in open boats, soaked and frostbitten, they landed on Elephant Island.
Solid ground at last.
For the first time in sixteen months. But it was an uninhabited rock, far from any shipping route. Nobody would ever look for them there.

chapters.heading: The James Caird
image_queries: James Caird lifeboat launching Elephant Island

lines.t: The nearest help was back where they started. The whaling stations of South Georgia, about thirteen hundred kilometres away, across the stormiest ocean on Earth.
In a lifeboat.
The largest one, the James Caird. Less than seven metres long. The ship's carpenter raised its sides and built a makeshift deck from wood and canvas.
Shackleton took five men. The most important was Frank Worsley, the captain of Endurance, a brilliant navigator.
How do you navigate a lifeboat in a storm?
With a sextant, when you can see the sun. In sixteen days, Worsley managed only a handful of sightings, braced against the mast while others held him.

They were constantly wet. Ice built up on the boat and had to be chipped off before it capsized them. At one point Shackleton saw what he took for a clearing sky. It was the white crest of an enormous wave.
And Worsley found the island.
A speck in the ocean. If he had missed it, the next land was Africa.
They landed in May 1916. On the wrong side of the island.
Of course they did.
The whaling stations were on the north coast. Between them lay mountains and glaciers that nobody had ever crossed. The boat was too damaged to sail around.
Shackleton, Worsley and a seaman named Tom Crean set off on foot. They had a rope, a carpenter's tool as an ice axe, and screws from the boat pushed through their boot soles for grip.
No tent?
No tent, no sleeping bags. They walked for thirty-six hours almost without stopping.
At one point, stuck high on a ridge with night coming, they coiled the rope, sat on it, and slid down the mountain in the dark.
And then?
On the morning of the 20th of May they heard a steam whistle. The factory whistle at the Stromness whaling station, calling men to work.
When they walked in, filthy and bearded, the station manager did not recognise the man he had met a year and a half earlier. Shackleton had to say his name.
What about the twenty-two men on Elephant Island?
They were living under two overturned boats, under Shackleton's deputy, Frank Wild. Every morning Wild told them to pack up, because the boss might come today.
How long did they wait?
Four and a half months. Shackleton tried three times with borrowed ships. Each time the ice turned him back.
The fourth attempt was in a small Chilean tug called the Yelcho. On the 30th of August 1916 she reached the island.
And he counted them.
From the boat, as he came in. All twenty-two. He later wrote to his wife: "Not a life lost, and we have been through Hell."
It is fair to add that the expedition had a second team, laying supplies on the far side of Antarctica. Three of those men died.
Shackleton returned south once more, and died of a heart attack at South Georgia in 1922. He is buried there, at Grytviken.
And the ship?
For more than a century, Endurance lay somewhere under the Weddell Sea ice. In March 2022 an expedition found her.

She sits upright, three thousand metres down, astonishingly well preserved in the cold. The name is still clear across the stern. She was only a few kilometres from the position Worsley wrote down in 1915.
With a sextant, on drifting ice.
What stays with me is the whistle. Thirty-six hours of walking, and then a factory whistle.
And the man who, every morning, told twenty-one others to pack their bags.
Would you have followed Shackleton?
